newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus leader takes domestic fight to Russia Duma.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader takes domestic fight to Russia Duma.

text.p: Embattled Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko took a fight against his political foes to the Russian parliament on Wednesday, provoking a walkout by liberal deputies.

Lukashenko, locked in a struggle with his own parliament, got a warm welcome from most Russian deputies who share his nostalgia for the Soviet Union and desire for closer integration between the two neighbouring states.
But some were more critical. Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the liberal Yabloko party, accused Lukashenko of using integration as a cloak for setting up a "totalitarian regime".
Mikhail Lapshin, head of the conservative Agrarian Party, said he was concerned about Lukashenko's confrontational tone and his intolerance of political opposition.
Back home in Minsk, his opponents scorned his speech. Former parliament speaker Stanislav Shushkevich said: "Lukashenko was stupid to address the Russian Duma and not his own parliament."
Current Speaker Semyon Sharetsky criticised the president for presenting himself as the sole supporter of close ties with Russia in Belarus.

Lukashenko proposed a joint session of the Russian and Belarussian parliaments in January to consider further moves towards union but did not fulfil Moscow press predictions that he would urge a confederation of the two countries.
Last April Lukashenko and President Boris Yeltsin agreed to link Belarus and Russia in a "community" but Lukashenko said that since then the project had failed to make progress.
He told his audience it was "now or never" for the seven-month-old partnership. "Either we get our community on its feet or we discredit the very idea of integration," he said.

Yegor Stroyev, chairman of the Federation Council, Russia's upper chamber, reacted coolly, saying it was better to wait until "political passions" in Belarus had calmed down before pushing for more closer ties. "We will have to wait a bit," he told Interfax news agency.
As Lukashenko began his speech to the Duma, Russia's lower house, Yabloko deputies walked out.
Yavlinsky warned that there was a danger of a repetition in Belarus of the violent clashes between Russia's president and parliament in Moscow in October 1993.

Belarussians will vote on November 24 in a referendum in which Lukashenko is seeking to broaden his powers while parliament wants to restrict them. "It is in fact a vote of confidence in Lukashenko," the Belarussian leader said.
The country's top electoral officer described Lukashenko's referendum on Monday as a "national disgrace" and accused the president of violating the law.
Lukashenko said his opponents, Western countries and some influential individuals in Russia were trying to use pressure against him, but did not name any names.

He later met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, who told him that Belarus must stick to the agreed schedule for handing over the last nuclear missiles on its territory to Russia.
In his speech Lukashenko suggested that the missile handover might be delayed and said Belarus could be a strategic ally for Russia if NATO expansion went ahead.
He coupled his attacks on the West and NATO with complaints about Russian newspapers and TV, which he said were spreading slander and disinformation about him.
Economic reformers in Russia believe full union with Belarus would be against Moscow's interests because of the weak state of its economy and the lack of progress towards a free market.
But Lukashenko indignantly denied this, saying lack of privatisation in Belarus did not mean the economy was in poor shape.
